speaker: nadia
text: Morning all. Kicking off planning for the harbor release and the workshop paper. Can we use this thread to get deadline, release version, and compute needs all pinned down in one place? I'd rather not chase them across DMs again.

speaker: felix
text: Works for me. On the release side, the main blocker is the sandbox image rebuild, since a dependency pin broke a few of the Rust tasks. I'll put the changelog draft in this thread once that's sorted so everyone can check it.

speaker: marcus
text: On the Rust breakage: are those the same tasks that got flagged in the last contamination pass? If we're rebuilding the image anyway, I'd like to swap out the two that have near-duplicates in a public repo before we freeze anything.

speaker: yuki
text: Quick check while we're pinning things down: is the harbor workshop paper submission deadline Oct 23? React 👍 if that matches your understanding.

speaker: elena
text: Once the image is rebuilt I'll need to rerun the Rust tasks end to end anyway. Do we know yet if swapping any out changes how many agent runs per task we want? That's what drives how much of the queue I have to block off.

speaker: yuki
text: Swapping tasks shouldn't change the per-task run count by itself, but the Rust ones worry me. If the build flakes under the new image, the pass rate gets noisy, so I'd like a quick pilot on them before we lock the run count.

speaker: felix
text: Version call so the changelog has a target: we're shipping this as harbor v1.2. The image rebuild and any Rust task swaps from Marcus go into that, so v1.2 stays frozen until the pilot comes back clean.

speaker: marcus
text: I ran the near-duplicate check on the Rust set again. The two I'm worried about have helper functions that match a popular crate's test suite almost line for line, so I'll draft replacement candidates from repos with clearer licenses and post them here for Yuki to look at.

speaker: theo
text: For the pilot I can reuse my baseline harness on the Rust tasks. Last time two of them timed out on cold cargo builds, so I'd cache the registry in the image or we'll be measuring download speed instead of the agent.

speaker: nadia
text: Good, that covers the image and the Rust pilot. Separate question: who's going to own the eval compute reservation for harbor? I want one name on it before we go further.

speaker: elena
text: I'll take it.

speaker: theo
text: Re the cargo cache: I can bake the registry into the pilot image and diff cold vs warm builds on the two that timed out. If the gap is big we should say so in the paper's setup section, since people will hit the same thing running it locally.

speaker: yuki
text: Agree on flagging it in the setup section. I'd also want the pilot to report build time separately from agent time, so the cold-vs-warm gap doesn't get folded into the pass rate.

speaker: marcus
text: Seconding the separate build-time reporting. Once the replacement Rust candidates are up, I'll note which ones pull in heavy crates so Theo can check whether they make the cold-build problem worse.

speaker: elena
text: If the pilot needs the cached registry baked in, I'll want that image tag from Theo before I queue anything. Otherwise my reruns will hit the cold builds and the numbers won't compare.

speaker: theo
text: Yep, I'll push the cached-registry image once the rebuild finishes and drop the tag here. One thing I noticed in my old harness logs: the two slow tasks also re-fetch git dependencies, not just crates.io, so I'll vendor those too or the warm builds will still look slower than they should.

speaker: theo
text: I'm scheduling my baseline reruns around the paper being due Oct 30. If the vendored image lands this week, I can finish the pilot and the full baseline table with a few days of slack before then.

speaker: felix
text: On vendoring the git deps: I'll check that the image build can reach those repos at build time. If it can't, cargo might quietly fall back to fetching at runtime and we'd be back to the same slow warm builds. I'll also add a line to the changelog draft about the cached registry.

speaker: yuki
text: For the pilot readout I'd like per-task pass rates on the Rust tasks with bootstrap intervals, not just the aggregate. That way we can see whether a flaky task is failing on the build or on the agent.

speaker: elena
text: For the per-task breakdown I'll keep the raw per-run logs with the cargo exit code split out from the test exit code. That way a build failure never gets counted as an agent failure when Theo builds the table.

speaker: yuki
text: Good. Can we also log wall-clock timeouts as their own category? An agent that runs out its time budget in a cargo build isn't a build failure or a test failure, and I don't want it landing in either bucket in the per-task intervals.

speaker: theo
text: Fine by me, I'll add a timeout flag to the harness output so those runs get their own column. I'd also record whether the timeout hit during the cargo build or after tests had started, since those read pretty differently.

speaker: marcus
text: One more column worth having: which crate each Rust task's tests lean on. If a flaky task turns out to share a dependency with one of the near-duplicate ones, that tells me whether the contamination and the build noise have the same cause.

speaker: yuki
text: Marcus, the dependency column is a good idea. I'd also tag whether each task's tests are pure unit tests or spin up something like a tempdir or a subprocess, since those are the ones I'd expect to flake independent of the agent.

speaker: elena
text: Fair warning, with all these flake categories the eval jobs are going to have more retries than I have gym visits this month.

speaker: yuki
text: Ha, fair. For the retries, can we log attempt number per run and only score the final attempt? Otherwise a task that needs a few tries to get past a tempdir flake looks cleaner than it really is.

speaker: theo
text: Final-attempt scoring works for me, but I'd also put the attempt-number distribution per task in an appendix table. Otherwise a tempdir task that passes on try three looks the same as one that passes first time, and readers can't tell which ones are flaky.

speaker: marcus
text: Good call on the appendix table. Once it exists I can cross-check the tempdir-flaky tasks against my dependency column, and if the same ones also sit near the duplicates, we'd want to mention that in the contamination section.

speaker: felix
text: For the appendix table I'll make the harness emit attempt number and the timeout flag as plain fields in the results JSON, so Theo's table script doesn't have to parse them out of the logs. I'll note the new fields in the changelog draft too.

speaker: yuki
text: Since the results JSON will carry the attempt number, can the plot show per-task pass rate on first attempt next to the final-attempt score? A big gap between the two bars would flag a flaky task at a glance, and it gives us a clean sentence for the paper's limitations paragraph.

speaker: nadia
text: I like the first-attempt vs final-attempt bars, that's an easy figure for readers to parse. Let's keep the plot caption blunt about what each bar means so nobody reads the gap as agent skill.

speaker: theo
text: For the caption I'll sort the bars by the first-vs-final gap instead of alphabetically, so the flaky tempdir ones cluster on one side. I'm guessing the subprocess tasks will stick out the most, but we'll see once the logs are in.

speaker: yuki
text: Sorting by the gap works for me, but I'd print the bootstrap interval on each bar too. A task with only a few runs can show a huge gap just from noise, and we shouldn't call it flaky on that alone.

speaker: marcus
text: Agree on the intervals. For the tasks with few runs I'd rather the caption say 'insufficient runs to call flaky' than leave a bare bar, so nobody quotes the gap as a finding. I can draft that wording for the limitations paragraph if it helps.

speaker: elena
text: If the caption is going to say 'insufficient runs', I should log the run count per task right next to the attempt number. Otherwise someone has to recount from the raw logs every time the plot regenerates.

speaker: felix
text: Easy enough, I'll add a run count field next to attempt number in the results JSON so the plot script can read it straight off. I'll put it in the changelog draft with the others.

speaker: yuki
text: With run count in the JSON I can also set a floor in the plot script so bars under it get greyed out automatically. I'd rather the figure show which bars we trust than rely on us remembering to caveat each one in the caption.

speaker: theo
text: Greyed-out bars work for me. I'll keep the sort by gap but push the greyed ones to the far end, so the flaky-looking ones we actually trust sit together and the noisy ones don't read as a trend.

speaker: nadia
text: Good, that settles the figure. Marcus, go ahead and draft the limitations wording, and make sure it says plainly that the greyed bars are excluded from any flakiness claim.

speaker: nadia
text: Morning all. Before we lock the paper outline I want to settle two things in this thread: what exactly gates a harbor release, and what goes in the held-out split. Marcus, can you start with where we are on licensing for the repo-sourced tasks? I'd rather find out now if any of them are a problem.

speaker: elena
text: anyone else seeing the scheduler drop jobs mid-queue? Two of my harbor baseline runs just vanished from the queue with no error, they never even got a worker.

speaker: marcus
text: Mostly fine, but a few of the repo-sourced tasks are a problem. Some come from repos with no license file at all, and a couple are GPL, which makes redistributing the full repo snapshot with the task murky. I'd like to go through those one by one before we call any of them safe for the held-out split.

speaker: felix
text: For the GPL ones, could we ship just the task spec plus a pinned commit hash and have the harness pull the repo at build time? That way we're not redistributing the snapshot ourselves. Not sure it fixes the no-license repos though.

speaker: marcus
text: Pinned hash helps with the GPL ones as far as I can tell, though I'd want to confirm the harness fetch doesn't count as us distributing anything. For the no-license repos it doesn't change much, since no license means all rights reserved by default. I'd lean toward dropping those from held-out unless we can get a maintainer to say yes.

speaker: yuki
text: On the gate itself: the harbor release gate threshold is 70% pass@1. Happy to defend that number in the paper once the licensing cuts settle what's actually in the split.

speaker: theo
text: If we drop the no-license repos from held-out, my baseline table is going to shift, a couple of those were tasks where the weaker models did oddly well. I'd want to rerun before we quote any numbers in the paper.

speaker: yuki
text: Also, that number is measured on the held-out set only, not dev, so Theo's rerun matters for it.

speaker: elena
text: If it's only the affected tasks we can rerun just those instead of the whole sweep, which is way easier to schedule. Theo, which models did oddly well on them? I'd start with those.

speaker: marcus
text: To give Theo and Elena a fixed target for the rerun: the held-out set is 1,200 items, counted after the no-license repos come out. I'll send the list of affected tasks shortly.

speaker: theo
text: Mostly the small open-weights code models, they nailed a few of the string-parsing tasks that the bigger ones fumbled. Honestly smells like memorization of those repos, so I'll start the rerun with those and flag anything that looks off.

speaker: theo
text: yeah, I think I hit that yesterday. One of my baseline jobs showed up as pending, then just disappeared an hour later. I figured I'd fat-fingered a cancel, but now I'm not so sure.

speaker: marcus
text: That memorization hunch is worth chasing. When I send the affected task list I'll add which repos are old enough to have been all over the web, so you can see if the weak-model wins line up with that.

speaker: elena
text: Once Marcus's list lands I'll tag those tasks in the scheduler so the rerun only picks up the affected ones. Theo, do you want the small open-weights models queued first, or all of them in one batch?

speaker: theo
text: Small open-weights first, since that's where the weird wins are. If they drop back to what we'd expect, I'll queue the bigger models after as a sanity check.

speaker: marcus
text: Also on my side: I'll finish the license review for the scraped repositories by Fri Oct 9, so the affected task list and the keep/drop calls will all come out of that pass.

speaker: yuki
text: If the small models drop back after the rerun, I'd like a quick contamination probe on those string-parsing tasks too, like checking whether they can complete the function body from just the file header. That would give us something concrete to cite in the paper instead of just calling it a hunch.

speaker: theo
text: Header-completion probe works for me, easy to bolt onto the rerun harness. I'd run it on a few of the bigger models too so we've got a contrast column, otherwise the small-model numbers don't mean much on their own.

speaker: elena
text: Mine had the same pattern, pending then gone. I'm checking whether it lines up with the preemption sweep, since both of ours were low priority.

speaker: elena
text: Header-completion probe is cheap to run, it's just short prompts with no tool calls. I'll give it its own job tag so it doesn't get mixed in with the pass-rate reruns when we pull results.

speaker: felix
text: Side note on the pinned-hash idea: if a maintainer force-pushes or deletes a repo, the harness fetch breaks at build time. We'd probably need some fallback or a clear failure message, otherwise someone's release build dies on a 404 with no explanation.

speaker: marcus
text: Good catch. A fallback mirror on our side would be redistribution again, which is the thing we're trying to avoid for the GPL repos. A clear failure message that names the repo and the pinned hash seems safer, so someone can chase it down themselves.

speaker: theo
text: That fits, mine was low priority too. I submitted it right after a batch of the higher-priority eval jobs went in, so a sweep bumping it would make sense. Is there a log for the sweep, or does it just silently requeue and lose the job?

speaker: felix
text: Agreed on the explicit failure message, I'll add it to the build step. Also, so nobody mixes the numbers up: the internal harbor-lite smoke set has 200 items, and that's a separate set from held-out. I'll run the fetch-failure check against it first since it's quick.

speaker: yuki
text: For the paper wording, I'd like the contamination section to report the header-completion results per task family, not one pooled number. If the string-parsing tasks are the only ones where the small models look suspicious, a pooled figure would hide that.

speaker: theo
text: Per-family works for me, I'll split the probe results by task family in the table. Fair warning, a couple of the families are tiny, so the per-family rates will be noisy and we should say that in the text.

speaker: elena
text: There's a sweep log but it only records jobs it successfully requeues, so a dropped one wouldn't show up. I'm grepping the scheduler's own debug output for the job IDs now to see if the requeue step threw anything.

speaker: nadia
text: For the tiny families, can we show confidence intervals next to the rates, or fold the smallest ones into an "other" row? Reviewers will poke at a 3-task family showing 100%. Theo, maybe mock up both versions and we can see which reads better.

speaker: yuki
text: I'd lean toward the intervals over an "other" row, since folding families together hides exactly the string-parsing split we care about. If we use Wilson intervals the 3-task family at 100% will at least show a lower bound that's honest about how little that tells us.

speaker: theo
text: Good call on grepping the debug output. If you find a requeue exception, send me the job IDs and I'll check whether mine threw the same thing. I still have the submit logs from the batch I launched right before it vanished.

speaker: theo
text: Wilson works for me, it's one line in the plotting script. I'll mock up both versions with the string-parsing family called out in its own row so we can compare how they read.

speaker: marcus
text: One caveat for the probe: a few of the string-parsing tasks come from small utility files that get vendored into lots of other repos. A model could have seen them under a different repo name, so a clean result on the original repo wouldn't rule out contamination. I'll mark those tasks in my notes so the paper doesn't read the probe as repo-specific.

speaker: elena
text: Found something. The debug output has a requeue failure on both of my job IDs, looks like a timeout talking to the quota service right when the sweep fires. Sending you the IDs so you can check yours against it.

speaker: yuki
text: Good point on the vendored utility files. Could we add a second probe variant that strips the repo-specific header and only gives the function signature? If the small models still complete the body, that points at the code itself being memorized rather than the repo.

speaker: theo
text: Signature-only variant is easy to add as a second prompt template. One catch is that some of the string-parsing functions have really generic names like split_lines, so a model might complete them from habit and not memory. I'd add a control with renamed signatures to see how much of the completion is just the obvious implementation.

speaker: yuki
text: Renamed-signature control makes sense. I'd want the renames to keep the argument types and docstring intact, otherwise a drop in completion could just mean the prompt got worse. Maybe also score by whether the body passes the task's tests, not by string match against the original.

speaker: marcus
text: License review for the scraped repositories is done, and three repos are excluded. I'm updating the affected task list now so it reflects those drops, and I'll send it with the old-repo notes and the vendored-file flags.

speaker: theo
text: Scoring by the task tests is cleaner, but a few of the string-parsing tasks have pretty loose tests where a naive split-and-strip body passes. That could inflate completion in the renamed control too. I'll flag those so we can report them separately.

speaker: yuki
text: Yes, report the loose-test ones separately. For the probe only, we could also run those bodies against a stricter check with CRLF line endings, empty input, and runs of repeated whitespace. A naive split-and-strip would fail that, and a memorized body would still pass. I wouldn't touch the actual benchmark tests for this.

speaker: theo
text: Stricter check is fine for the probe, but I'd run the original reference bodies through it first. If some of the upstream implementations are naive too, they'd fail on CRLF or empty input, and then a memorized body failing wouldn't tell us anything. I can split those out as their own bucket.

speaker: theo
text: Got the IDs. Checked mine against them and the same quota service timeout shows up on my job right at the sweep, so that's the cause. Probably worth a ticket asking for the requeue to retry instead of just dropping the job.

speaker: yuki
text: Yes, validate the stricter check against the reference bodies first. If some upstream ones fail it, I'd rather swap in a patched reference for the probe than drop the task, as long as the patch only handles the edge cases and doesn't change the core logic. We should note that in the methods text.

speaker: theo
text: Patched references for the probe are fine as long as we log which tasks got one. Also, I put the release gate in the draft's methods section as 75% pass@1, so the probe text can point back to it.

speaker: elena
text: For the signature-only and renamed-signature runs I'll give each prompt template its own job tag, same as the header probe. Otherwise the outputs blur together when I pull results. The bigger-model contrast runs will go under their own tags too.

speaker: elena
text: Agreed, I'll file it with the scheduler folks and attach both sets of IDs plus the timeout trace. In the meantime I'm resubmitting my baselines at normal priority so the sweep leaves them alone.

speaker: nadia
text: Thinking about the contamination section layout: maybe lead with a short paragraph on what the probe can and can't tell us, then the per-family table. Otherwise reviewers will read the header-completion numbers as proof of memorization instead of a signal.

speaker: felix
text: Unrelated to the probe layout, but for the release tag I'm leaning toward v1.3 for harbor once the license drops and the hash-pinning change are in. Just a tentative idea, nothing decided, so shout if you'd rather bump it differently.

speaker: theo
text: Same here, I'll bump mine to normal priority and resubmit. I'll also add a quick check to my launch script that flags any job still missing from the queue after a few minutes, so a silent drop doesn't cost me another day.

speaker: theo
text: For the layout in 37, I can put a dagger on the vendored-file tasks and a different symbol on the patched-reference ones. Then the caveat paragraph can point at the table rows directly instead of describing them in prose.

speaker: yuki
text: Dagger and a second symbol works for me. I'd add a short footnote under the table saying the vendored-file rows can't be read as repo-specific, so nobody has to hunt for it in the caveat paragraph.

speaker: nadia
text: Morning all. Marcus's contamination check from Friday came back with overlap, so harbor is moving to a new version and we need to rerun all the baselines on it. Felix, can you start sketching what the release looks like? Theo and Elena, let's sort out what the reruns will cost us in compute.

speaker: felix
text: Sketching it now. Rough shape is to drop the overlapping tasks, pull replacements from the held-out pool, and rebuild the docker images so the pinned commits don't carry the upstream fixes. Marcus, did the overlap cluster in particular repos or was it spread out?

speaker: marcus
text: Mostly clustered. The bulk of the hits are in the web framework repos and one CLI-parsing library, where the fix diffs got mirrored in tutorial posts and gists. There are a few stragglers elsewhere, so I'd want to run the same check on the replacements from the held-out pool before we trust them.

speaker: elena
text: On the compute side, the web framework images are the slow ones to rebuild since they pull a ton of deps. Theo, can you share the per-model wall-clock and token numbers from the last baseline pass? I'll scale the reruns off those.

speaker: theo
text: Pulling them now. Heads up that the last pass logged tokens before retries for a couple of models, so the raw totals undercount. The web framework tasks were also where most of the timeouts happened, so I'd pad those when you scale.

speaker: felix
text: Thanks both. I'm going with what I proposed on Wed Oct 7 for the release plan, and I'm starting on it now. Marcus, I'll start with the web framework and CLI-parsing clusters and send you the replacement candidates for the contamination check.

speaker: yuki
text: One thing to watch with the swaps: if the held-out replacements skew easier than the web framework tasks they replace, the rerun numbers won't be comparable to the old baselines. Felix, can you tag each replacement with the task it stands in for? Then I can compare difficulty per cluster.

speaker: marcus
text: +1 to Yuki's tagging. One wrinkle: the held-out pool is light on routing and middleware bugs and heavy on templating fixes, so some dropped tasks won't have a like-for-like stand-in. Felix, if you tag the closest match, can you also flag where the bug type differs? Then Yuki can treat those separately.

speaker: felix
text: Yes, I can add both fields to the manifest, a stand-in ID and a bug-type flag. For the routing and middleware gaps I'll mark the nearest templating or request-parsing task as a loose match so Yuki can bucket those separately.

speaker: yuki
text: Sounds good, that works for bucketing. I'm updating the eval config now to point at v1.3 so the pass criteria and the per-cluster comparison both key off the new manifest fields.

speaker: elena
text: For the web framework rebuilds I can try one shared base layer for the dependency install, so only the repo checkout differs per task. That should cut most of the slow part, unless the pinned commits need conflicting dep versions. Felix, will the replacement tasks pin different versions of the framework?

speaker: felix
text: Mostly the same pins, but a few of the templating replacements come from an older major line of the framework, so one shared layer will probably break for those. Two base layers might cover it. I'll check the dep manifests on the candidates and flag which ones diverge.

speaker: elena
text: Works for me. If the older-line ones need an older Python too, that layer gets heavier, so flag the interpreter requirement along with the framework pin. I'd rather build that separately than patch around it per task.

speaker: marcus
text: Heads up on the older-major-line templating candidates: old-version blog posts and Q&A threads are everywhere, so I'd expect more overlap there than in the newer-line ones. Felix, can you send those first so I can run the check on them before the rest?

speaker: felix
text: Makes sense, I'll pull the older-line templating ones out and send those to you ahead of the rest. I'll include the interpreter requirement in the same batch so Elena can see which ones would need the heavier layer.

speaker: theo
text: For the older-line templating ones, do the tests in those pinned repos run clean on the older interpreter? If a few fail at baseline I'd rather know before I burn model runs on them.

speaker: theo
text: Whatever the interpreter answer turns out to be, I'll rerun all baselines on harbor v1.3 by Fri Oct 16. I'll pad the web framework runs for timeouts and count tokens after retries this time.

speaker: felix
text: Checked a couple of the older-line templating repos just now. Their test suites import a stdlib module that was removed in newer interpreters, so they only run on the older one. I'll mark those in the manifest so Theo can run a smoke pass on them first.

speaker: elena
text: That settles the layer question then: the older-line ones get their own base image with the older interpreter. I'll key it off the interpreter flag in Felix's manifest so I'm not guessing which tasks belong in it.

speaker: nadia
text: While you sort the images, I'm drafting the contamination paragraph for the paper. Marcus, can you give me a plain-words description of how the fix diffs ended up mirrored in tutorials and gists? I'd like reviewers to see why the web framework and CLI-parsing repos got hit hardest.

speaker: marcus
text: Plain version: when a popular framework patches a bug, people write it up within days. Tutorials walk through the diff line by line and gists paste the patched function, so the fix text ends up all over the web. Those repos are widely taught and widely forked, which is why they got hit hardest. The CLI-parsing library is the same story, since its fixes show up as copy-paste snippets in how-to posts.

speaker: nadia
text: Thanks Marcus, that's exactly the framing I wanted for reviewers. Separately, the caption on the results table reads harbor v1.2, so I'll build the table around that label and slot Theo's numbers in as they land.

speaker: yuki
text: For the per-cluster figure I'm thinking paired bars, old tasks vs their stand-ins, with the loose-match bucket hatched so nobody reads it as like-for-like. If the hatched bars drift a lot from the solid ones, that's a caveat we should put in the text.

speaker: theo
text: For the paired bars, do you want one panel per model or pooled across models? The loose-match bucket is small, so per-model will probably be noisy there. I can produce either from the logs.

speaker: yuki
text: Pooled for the main figure, with bootstrap intervals resampled over tasks so the small loose-match bucket shows how wide it really is. Per-model panels can go in the appendix, mainly so we can check whether one model is driving any gap between the hatched and solid bars.

speaker: theo
text: For the bootstrap, should I collapse retries to one outcome per task before resampling, or treat each attempt as its own row? Collapsing is cleaner for the intervals, but it hides the flaky templating tasks.

speaker: yuki
text: Collapse to one outcome per task for the resampling, since tasks are the unit we're generalizing over. But keep the per-task pass fraction across attempts and show the flaky templating tasks in a separate small table so they don't disappear.

speaker: theo
text: Unrelated to the bootstrap, but who actually holds the compute reservation for the rerun? I want to make sure my web framework jobs are queued under the right one.

speaker: elena
text: That's me, the rerun reservation is under my name. Queue your web framework jobs there and ping me if they sit pending, since the older-interpreter image will need its own slot.

speaker: theo
text: For the flaky templating table, should a timeout during template compilation count as a fail in the pass fraction, or get its own column? Those feel different from a test actually failing.

speaker: yuki
text: Own column, I'd say. A compile timeout could be the model's edit causing a slow or looping template, or just a cold cache on the older image, and those mean different things. Can you log which stage each timeout hit so we can split them in the table?

speaker: theo
text: Should be doable, the harness already writes a stage marker before each step. I'll add a flag for first run on a fresh container so cold-cache timeouts separate from the model's edit causing a looping template.

speaker: elena
text: I can pre-warm the template compile cache when I bake the older-interpreter image, which should cut most of the cold-cache timeouts. Theo, keep the fresh-container flag anyway so we can see how big the gap is.

speaker: yuki
text: Good idea on the pre-warm. If the gap between warm and cold runs turns out to be tiny, we can say so in one sentence and drop the cold-cache caveat from the flaky table.

speaker: marcus
text: For the hatched loose-match bars, I can add a one-line reason per stand-in so reviewers see how it differs from the original. Some swap a routing off-by-one for a header-parsing bug in the same module, which isn't really like-for-like difficulty.

speaker: yuki
text: Marcus, can you also tag each stand-in with a short category, like same module but different bug class, or same bug class in a different file? Then we can check whether the drift in the hatched bars comes from one kind of swap, like the routing-to-header-parsing ones.

speaker: marcus
text: Sure. I'll add a third tag for stand-ins that keep the bug class but change the surrounding feature, like a decorator edge case swapped for a context-manager one. The tags can go in the same sheet as the one-line reasons, keyed by task id, so Theo can join them straight onto the results.

speaker: theo
text: Keyed by task id works for me. I'll join the tag sheet in the results notebook so the hatched bars can be split by swap type, and the decorator-to-context-manager ones get their own color.

speaker: yuki
text: Nice, a separate color for the decorator-to-context-manager swaps will make it obvious if that group is dragging the hatched bars. If it is, I'd rather say so plainly in the text than average it into the pooled number.

speaker: nadia
text: Works for me. I'll write the figure caption so the hatched bars are explained as loose-match stand-ins, and leave a placeholder sentence for the swap-type breakdown until Theo's split shows what the decorator-to-context-manager group does.

speaker: yuki
